Current Independent Project

Independent Game Project — Developer and AI Systems Designer

September 2026–Present | Godot 4 survival game in development

Design and direct a multi-agent development system for a third-person post-apocalyptic survival game. Own architecture, work allocation, review criteria, acceptance decisions, and iteration priorities; AI agents write most of the code. The game has not been released.

Architecture: treating AI collaboration as an engineering team
  • Designed three persistent Claude roles covering process and cost, content-production dispatch, and servers/game systems, alongside three Codex execution accounts and Gemini CLI. Separated decision-making, implementation, and review responsibilities; evolved the architecture through more than five iterations in a month from one coordinating conversation to delegated roles.
  • Configured up to 15 concurrent conversations per Codex account. This is configured capacity, not sustained utilization or verified throughput. Personally owned architecture, operating rules, acceptance criteria, and decisions; AI agents wrote most of the code.
End-to-end dispatch and traceable delivery
  • Decomposed goals into initiatives, acceptance-ready work packages, and execution tasks (G/M/W). A unified dispatch entry point selects account, model, and reasoning level from available quota and task difficulty, links each dispatch to its parent requirement, and creates execution records.
  • Designed a dispatch → initial check → independent review → installation → repeated verification → status-update workflow. Database-backed progress views separate decisions requiring human judgment. The November 3, 2026 snapshot lists 31 initiatives and 401 work packages, with 197 marked complete; approximately 2,100 Codex dispatches logged since October 27 measure activity, not completed requirements.
Go orchestration service and incremental migration
  • Led AI-assisted development of a single Go orchestration service to progressively consolidate hundreds of persistent Python scripts. Modules cover event-hook dispatch, Codex app-server conversation control, dispatch state machines, mailboxes, scheduling, health checks, subprocess supervision, and memory limits.
  • Captured legacy inputs and outputs as golden samples, compared Go and Python behavior, and used a three-stage rollout with rollback paths. Project statistics report 35 internal packages, approximately 131,000 non-test lines, and 410 test files. The core migration has 48 work packages marked complete; remaining scripts are still being migrated. Code volume and test-file counts are not coverage or pass-rate measures.
Inter-agent communication and work continuity
  • Replaced file-based messages with PostgreSQL role mailboxes, adding receipt monitoring, uncollected-message alerts, and wake-up handling. Reserved a fallback channel for urgent work and outages to reduce interruptions. Logged tool calls and failures for later investigation.
  • Designed automatic context compression, rolling handoff documents, and A/B handovers for primary roles, preserving task IDs, file locations, and pending responses. Database checks prevent two primary instances from becoming active simultaneously. Documented recovery of applications, database services, schedules, and mailboxes after reboot; long-running operation is a design goal, not a verified availability SLA.
Quality gates, failure handling, and acceptance
  • Used Gemini for an initial read-only check with spot verification, followed by independent Claude Opus and Codex reviews. Integration requires both reviews and self-tests to pass. Later review rounds focus on major issues, with simplified alternatives escalated when work repeatedly fails review.
  • Designed detection, interruption, and restart handling for stalled execution; repeated errors trigger a different approach on the third occurrence. Pre/post-tool hooks constrain role responsibilities, scanning scope, and test behavior. Periodic maintenance turns newly discovered failure modes into future checks.
  • Queued Godot tests with resource prechecks and headless automation, while requiring server-connected conditions for performance measurement. Headless success is not visual acceptance. Character animation, the server-connected game build, and the 60 FPS target remain in progress.
Data-informed model routing and quota management
  • Analyzed account-quota changes across 541 dispatches, estimating roughly 6.2%, 1.1%, and 0.2% of weekly quota per task for high-, upper-mid-, and mid-tier models. These are order-of-magnitude comparisons: concurrent work can be counted more than once, so they are not precise per-task token or billing costs.
  • Reserved high-tier models for first-of-a-kind difficult work, reused review conversations, and routed small changes to lighter models. Non-LLM scripts select full-speed, normal, or economy modes from remaining quota and reset timing, with low-quota pause, handoff, and recovery handling. A 70–80% reduction in high-tier usage is projected, not measured savings or a throughput guarantee.
Knowledge engineering and AI content pipelines
  • Built a three-layer rules index → topic files → evidence structure, more than ten topic knowledge bases, 47 Claude skills, approximately 90 project rules, and vector memory. Converted recurring dispatch, review, inventory, and handoff work into reusable procedures.
  • Integrated NVIDIA Kimodo motion generation and standard skeletons, MotionBricks transition baking, Tripo 3D, Blender MCP, ComfyUI, Gemini image generation, and ElevenLabs audio. Defined machine-checkable standards for polygon counts, UVs, open edges, and color palettes.
  • Project records report review and triage of approximately 850 environment textures and 307 sound assets, alongside building dimensions, monster inventories, and game-balance validation specifications. Reviewed assets do not imply that all assets are shipped or the game is complete.

Judgment and execution: from constraints to the next validation

Diagnose the constraint before scaling collaboration | Mid-September–early October
  • Started with one Claude coordinator and one Codex implementer exchanging Markdown messages. As files grew, repeated reading consumed more context and new conversations lost continuity. Identified information retention and handoff design, not just model capability, as the constraint; bounded open messages and file size before redesigning communication.
Separate knowledge access and responsibility | October 11–20
  • Reorganized scattered rules into an index → topic files → evidence hierarchy and converted recurring mistakes into reusable procedures. When initial checks produced unreliable evidence, limited that role to read-only work and spot-checked its output rather than treating model statements as verification.
  • A single conversation handling dispatch, review, and process control created context pressure and self-review risk. Split these responsibilities across three persistent roles. Project records describe two successful A/B handover tests; a later failure exposed lost in-flight subagent work, prompting a requirement to deliver or hand off before clearing a conversation, enforced with a hook.
Replace reminders with traceable coordination | October 22–25
  • Replaced fragile file mailboxes and direct messaging calls with background delivery and PostgreSQL mailboxes, including receipt tracking and uncollected-message alerts. Stopped idle backup conversations from waiting continuously for mail and documented reboot recovery, balancing continuity against quota consumption.
Instrument first, then optimize | October 27–30
  • Recorded dispatches in a database before comparing execution and usage. Replaced a costly, slow multi-seat art voting process with author self-checks and an initial check, while retaining independent cross-review for code integration. Converted approved plans into owned tasks immediately instead of leaving them only in documents.
Shrink the rollout unit after failures | October 31–November 3
  • A growing fleet of persistent Python scripts increased memory pressure and debugging cost. Led consolidation into a Go service using captured legacy inputs/outputs, behavioral comparisons, and staged rollback. Project records describe repeated installation failures, including memory exhaustion, followed by fallback to the previous implementation.
  • Adjusted execution to migrate one script at a time, observe it for ten minutes, and retain the old implementation only where problems remained. Prioritized reversible changes over a single all-at-once cutover. These are source-reported recovery experiences, not independently verified zero-downtime or production-availability claims.
Let tests override review opinions and bound review loops
  • A review had judged a change unaffected, but subsequent tests failed in three areas. Prioritized actual runtime results and post-write readback over model assertions; used real screenshots for UI decisions and required server-connected performance measurements. Headless tests do not establish visual acceptance.
  • One work item accumulated as many as 25 review tickets. Introduced a major-issues-only scope from round three and escalation of a simpler alternative when review continued to fail. Repeated errors trigger a different approach; unnecessary abstractions are removed to keep effort focused on verifiable core functionality.

Source scope: based on the author’s project record updated November 3, 2026. Statistics are source-reported; the database, source code, and test evidence were not independently re-audited. The game remains in development; these workflows and figures do not establish shipped-product reliability or performance.

03

Current Professional Case Study: AI-Assisted Backend Engineering

Existing Online-Game Platform — AI-Assisted Backend Workflow

Late July 2026–Present | Anonymized professional case study

Owned workflow design, boundary decisions, and the organization of repair and validation; AI participated in investigation, implementation, and testing. This describes personal decisions and iterations, not sole authorship of all code or acceptance of every repair in production.

Map the system before allowing changes
  • Since late July 2026, designed AI-assisted investigation, repair, local testing, and development-environment deployment workflows for an existing online-game platform. Used actual build and deployment configuration to distinguish active services from historical repositories. Required checks of remotes, versions, and uncommitted changes before work on isolated branches.
Load knowledge by task and separate discovery from repair
  • Repeatedly loading large rule sets increased context overhead. Introduced task-to-document routing and role-specific entry documents. Separated read-only investigation from repair decisions, triaging candidate findings rather than counting reports as completed fixes.
Track deduplication and coverage, not report volume
  • Repeated findings and uncertain scan coverage led to report fingerprints, evidence requirements, and explicit status transitions. Recorded clean scanned areas as well as findings. This public account describes methods only, without customer identities, internal service names, or vulnerability details.
Make test cleanup depend on ownership evidence
  • Used localhost binding, unique ports, task-specific directories, and ownership markers to protect shared environments. Resources are not deleted when ownership cannot be established. Cleanup runs after success, failure, or timeout, with port checks; cleanup failures are reported separately rather than replacing test outcomes. Later separated each agent’s test environment completely.
Migrate task storage without abandoning in-flight work
  • When moving file-based task management to PostgreSQL, took snapshots and rehearsed the schema before waiting for important in-flight work to finish. Retained migration archives and outcome records. Reused these reversible-migration lessons in the independent game’s mailbox and task systems.
Test current builds with fresh evidence and reduce operational overhead
  • After shared-module changes, pinned versions again, synchronized dependent repositories, and rebuilt rather than reusing stale binaries or evidence. Planned data collection before major test runs, used a fresh test-agent conversation, and added isolated analysis of the frozen version before testing.
  • When comprehensive pre-deployment backups became an operational burden, simplified that workflow around the last successful version and build identifier. Required a necessity check before introducing abstractions, caches, retries, or concurrency. These are context-specific workflow choices, not universal guidance to omit backups or a security guarantee.
Automate task closure while preserving change boundaries
  • Used isolated git worktrees and ownership markers for the task lifecycle. Incorporated new-branch pushes, evidence archiving, and cleanup into closure, while explicitly excluding force pushes, history rewrites, mainline merges, and remote-branch deletion.
In progress: isolate company and personal-project data
  • Work is ongoing to separate previously shared task-database areas and hooks. Changes are tested in a test database and cross-reviewed by two models; review exposed a remaining isolation-boundary issue that is still being corrected. Bringing personal-project quota optimizations back to the company workflow is a future step, not a completed outcome.

Based on the author’s work record updated November 3, 2026; company code, deployments, and test evidence have not been independently audited. Internal links, system-size figures, and specific vulnerability information are omitted.
